title: House of Chains
author: Steven Erikson
review:
**spoiler alert** Although I rated this a 3/5 and Gardens of the Moon a 4/5, I liked this entry more than the first, but my expectations have been adjusted as I've gotten deeper into the series.

Things I liked about this entry:

- Karsa Orlong: I enjoyed the focus on this character in the beginning and his overall arc in this entry. Having more time with a subset of the characters is why I liked Deadhouse Gates so much and the story is the strongest and most coherent when we're not constantly jumping around (although there is probably the most jumping around since Gardens in the second half of the book). Icarium vs Karsa was probably my favorite part of the book and made me really nervous since I'm a big fan of them both (and Mappo of course), I hope the series continues to have main characters at odds with each other. If anything, this novel could have been more aggressive with that, there seemed to be some pretty obvious baddies here on Shaik's side with Korbolo Dom and Bidithal, would be more interesting to have main characters be on opposite sides with a more dedicated view that their side is right.
- Theme and imagery: Just really strong images of chains and the thematic cohesion around slavery in society and to gods was really great here. I like this trend that Erikson has of making each entry thematically distinct while also adding little nuggets here and there of ice, dust, etc that you can guess are the thematic core of future entries based on their titles.
- Heboric: I'm really interested in the development in his character, and his dream / trip with the tea was one of my favorite parts of the series and seemed to really pull back the curtain on some of the larger conflicts going on in the series. Heboric just seems like a very flawed character but inherently good with an interesting background that makes for developments surrounding him to be unexpected.
- Larger scope: It's interesting that this series starts with a very narrow scope; a single character who is naive of the larger world, its history, and even themselves and then explodes into a multi-realm power struggle. Erikson comes close to tipping his hand here where you can see some of the larger threads of the story connecting between gods. I get the feeling that Osric, Cotillion, and some other gods that are alluded to will become bigger players in future entries.

Things I'm indifferent to:

- Crokus and Apsalar: Had potential, but kind of fell flat, not sure where they are really going and some of their time together wasn't that interesting, but I did like their interactions with Cotillion even though I don't really buy their relationship to him. Shouldn't Apsalar hate Cotillion? Especially after he possessed her and destroyed her whole fishing village?
- Shaik vs Tavore: Felt pretty anticlimactic after everything after the first book onward foreshadows the clash between them only to have it end so quickly and no real character developments follow from it. Felisin elder felt kind of wasted here, she didn't have many meaningful decisions to make and didn't seem to particularly take a stance about why the Malazan empire was evil.

Things I didn't like:

- Trull Sengar and Onrack: Just not very invested in this storyline and it wasn't particularly interesting. Hopefully the development of these characters continues more throughout the series to make sense of their appearance here. Was just pretty bored with their adventures in this one.
- Pearl and Lostara: Felt like a pretty pointless side quest here and wasted potential. Might have accomplished some world building, but I would have been fine with this being left out of the book. I was hoping for some interaction between Pearl and Kalam after their encounter in Deadhouse Gates.
